summary:
Imo State lies wholly inside Nigeria's national legal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) operates throughout the country and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. Sharia criminal law, under which male sodomy carries the death penalty, applies in twelve northern states and does not apply in Imo, a southern state.

Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under the shadow of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Where a trans person is detained, placement between male and female sections has been left to official discretion: press coverage of Bobrisky's 2024 imprisonment openly asked which prison the authorities would keep her in.

Police enforcement against same-sex conduct in Imo is active and documented. In April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found that the victims were themselves arrested by police and might need legal support. On 19 February 2025 the Imo Police Command reported foiling a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arresting a number of gay and lesbian suspects and placing fleeing attendees on a police search list.

Violence against LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria is met with official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Extortion and beatings by police for perceived sexual orientation are a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than creating it. The absence of any statutory protection means that hostile conduct by police or by private attackers in Imo has no hate-crime overlay to fall back on.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in the available sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender. The case is a currency-offence prosecution rather than a gender-identity offence, but it is the clearest available evidence of how a visibly trans detainee is processed.

The northern states present a materially harsher profile for onward travel within Nigeria than Imo does, since Sharia criminal law there carries the death penalty for male sodomy under state Zina provisions, while the secular maximum elsewhere is 14 years' imprisonment.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ+ residents of Imo State live under the SSMPA alongside the rest of Nigeria, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment available for cohabitation, public shows of affection and the operation of gay organisations, not only for sexual conduct. The 2018 case shows that accusation alone can trigger street violence and police processing at the same time, and that the accused may end up needing legal representation from local advocacy bodies such as NoStringsNG.

Local reporting in February 2025 framed a party in Orogwe as a same-sex gathering and published the arrests as a police success, indicating that residents who attend private social events risk being publicly identified as gay or lesbian suspects. Attendees who fled remained on a police search list, so the exposure did not end when the event broke up.

Residents also face community vigilantism independently of the state: in the 2018 incident the stripping, beating and parading was carried out in the street before police took the men into custody. Trans residents have no express statutory prohibition on their identity, but the unresolved cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters leave public gender expression legally unsettled, and there is no sourced protection against dismissal, eviction or family expulsion on grounds of gender identity.

Imo is outside the Sharia zone, so the twelve northern states' death-penalty provisions do not reach residents here; the national secular penalties and police practice are what apply.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted into law is not settled by the sources available here.

The outcome of the February 2025 Orogwe arrests is unresolved: whether charges were filed, how many attendees were charged, and whether those placed on the police search list were located is not sourced.

No sourced account of the legal outcome of the 2018 Imo street-parade case was available beyond the NoStringsNG inquiry into the victims' own arrest and possible need for legal support.

Imo State-level legislation or police directives specific to sexual orientation or gender identity are not sourced; the dossier rests on the national SSMPA, national press reporting and Imo Police Command statements.

Whether Nigerian authorities maintain any written policy on the placement of trans detainees in male or female prison sections is not sourced; the available evidence is press framing at sentencing and the October 2024 panel finding on Bobrisky's housing.
